newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge renew legacy of Cambodian discord.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge renew legacy of Cambodian discord.

text.p: Breakaway factions of the Khmer Rouge, architects of Cambodia's brutal "killing fields" regime of the late 1970s, appear to be rebuilding their political muscle even as their military might crumbles away.

Exploiting rifts within Cambodia's fragile coalition government, they have gained a foothold in the political power structure and once again have divided the nation against itself, political analysts said.

Support from Khmer Rouge defectors could be vital for Cambodia's two main political parties -- which jointly rule the country in an uneasy, sometimes fractious alliance -- as they battle to win sole power in elections expected next year.

"The breakaway Khmer Rouge have more leverage now because of the heightened tension between the two governing parties, who lobby to win them over to their respective sides," said Lao Mong Hay of the Khmer Institute of Democracy.
"If we are not united... and keep up this infighting, if I were a Khmer Rouge, I would stand back with my hands behind me and laugh," he added.

Cambodian and western analysts point to fighting this past week in the important northwest province of Battambang, where humn rights observers said forces loyal to First Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh clashed with followers of Second Premier Hun Sen, leaving 14 dead.

The dispute apparently erupted when soldiers from Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) feuded over a group of defectors from the Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-1979 regime left more than one million Cambodians dead from murder, malnutrition and overwork.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991, but later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition government which Ranariddh and Hun Sen formed after elections in 1993.

FUNCINPEC officials said the ex-Khmer Rouge of Samlaut had left the CPP-controlled Samlaut base in the northwest to join their side, but CPP officials said the troops were trying to rejoin Khmer Rouge hardliners.
Such conflicting accounts, born from competition between FUNCINPEC and CPP over defectors, have become increasingly familiar since August.
It was then that Ieng Sary, foreign minister and deputy premier in Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot's regime, broke with the hardliners. His move prompted thousands more defections.
The Maoist guerrilla movement has since dwindled to less than 2,000 hardliners based in Anlong Veng near the Thai border.

Since August, Ranariddh and Hun Sen have raced to add troops to their own sides, each offering many concessions. They convinced King Norodom Sihanouk to grant amnesty for Ieng Sary and gave defectors top positions in the armed forces.

In a sign that the competition is increasing with the demise of the hardliners, 15 FUNCINPEC officials made a risky trip to a village 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Anlong Veng last week to try to convince infamous Khmer Rouge commander Ta Mok, known as "the butcher," to defect.
"(The trip) is certainly a do-or-die effort. FUNCINPEC are behind the eight ball to pull it off," said one military analyst.
The high-stakes game courting ex-Khmer Rouge has prompted Sihanouk to assert that Ranariddh and Hun Sen were responsible for "the dying Khmer Rouge (being) saved from a certain death".

The policy followed by the co-premiers has given the Khmer Rouge a dangerous rebirth at a time when the rebels should be at their weakest, Sihanouk said in a written interview released at the weekend.

Despite his protests, the king is unlikely to intervene as he prefers to steer clear of the animosity between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, which is expected to worsen ahead of national elections scheduled for 1998, analysts said.
The parties of the two leaders will be striving to emerge from the elections with sole power, and both have wasted no time wooing Ieng Sary's Democratic National United Movement.
"The (Khmer Rouge) have become the king-makers, and they are increasingly skilled at pursuing their own agenda," said the military analyst, referring to the competition for their loyality.

While the ex-guerrillas are divided by party affiliation, Lao Mong Hay said, they are more united than the coalition government because they have a common goal: to exploit rifts and gain political muscle in Cambodia.
Therein lies the irony, analysts said -- a rebel movement that only months ago seemed destined for extinction is alive again.
"The Khmer Rouge were a dinosaur not so long ago. Now they're a living dinosaur," said one Cambodian analyst.
